list.listitem: Use clues from the history and physical examination to establish a presumptive diagnosis on which to base diagnostic testing. C

History and physical examination alone are often adequate to begin initial treatment for gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), dyspepsia, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), pelvic inflammatory disease, and urinary tract infection. C
Lipase and amylase are the best lab tests for diagnosing pancreatitis. C
Laboratory tests are not very helpful in diagnosing cholecystitis, appendicitis, or urolithiasis. C
Ultrasound is the best test if cholecystitis or ectopic pregnancy is suspected. C
CT scanning is the best test for possible appendicitis, intestinal obstruction, urolithiasis, diverticulitis, and abdominal aortic aneurysm. C

background.definition: Pain or any uncomfortable feeling in the abdominal region including the flank.

list.listitem: Based on data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), abdominal pain was the principle reason for 8.9% of all emergency department visits in 2021.
Accounted for 0.9% of all primary care office visits in 2019 per CDC data from the National Ambulatory Medical Survey .

Authors of a systematic review of 18 studies from 12 countries investigating reasons for visits in primary care found abdominal symptoms were not ranked among the top 12 reasons for visits reported by clinicians in either developed or undeveloped countries. However, using data reported by patients from 5 studies, an abdominal problem ranked third as reason for visit.

Twenty-two percent of adults have had abdominal pain severe enough to be reported to a physician or other professional, cause the patient to take medication, or substantially interfere with activities at some point in their life.
Approximately 2% of patients who present to the emergency department (ED) have small bowel obstruction.

In a meta-analysis of 14 studies on abdominal pain in primary care (excluding studies of children only), about 10% of patients had a serious, potentially surgical diagnosis. The most common diagnoses were gastroenteritis (7.2%-18.7%), irritable bowel syndrome (2.6%-13.2%), a urologic cause (4.1%-6.9%), or constipation (3.1%-6.2%).
In patients older than 60 years who presented to the emergency department with abdominal pain, 60% were hospitalized, 20% underwent surgery or other invasive treatment, and 5% died within 2 weeks.
Based on CDC data, abdominal pain was the 14th leading principle hospital discharge diagnosis in 2008 (262,000 visits or 1.6%).

In an observational study of 480 cases of acute abdominal pain presenting to a tertiary urban European emergency department, representing 12.1% of screened visits, an extra-abdominal cause was identified in 163 cases (43%), and 63 (13.1%) had a subsequent related representation, investigation, or surgery related to the index visit; the most prevalent causes of these were cholelithiasis, gastroenteritis, and urinary retention. A missed diagnosis was attributed to 27 (5.6%) of presentations.
The most common causes of abdominal pain in the primary care office and emergency department are shown in .

Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) causes abdominal pain in 2.7% (95% CI 2.0%-3.4%) to 6.2% (95% CI 2.6%-10.3%) of patients based on two meta-analyses, the former including 47 studies with 10,890 patients and the latter 12,797 patients. Most studies in the first paper were on hospitalized patients and studies in the second paper were noted to have high risk of bias. Other GI symptoms reported in patients with COVID-19 include diarrhea in 12.4% and 7.7%, and nausea and/or vomiting in 9.0% and 7.8%, respectively.

In another meta-analysis of three studies on abdominal pain in patients with COVID-19, abdominal pain was associated with illness severity; the odds ratio for patients with severe illness compared to non-severe patients was 7.17; 95% CI 1.95-26.34. GI symptoms do not appear to increase risk of death.
The abdomen is innervated by nociceptive afferent nerves. These nerves can be stimulated by stretching of visceral organs or inflammation of the peritoneal lining.
The pathophysiology of specific conditions such as cholecystitis and appendicitis is discussed in those chapters.

The most reliable history and physical examination clues for each of the most common causes of abdominal pain are outlined below: Pain usually of less than 48 hours duration (in alphabetical order):
Appendicitis: RLQ pain, migration of pain from periumbilical area to RLQ (if present, has the highest positive predictive value), fever, pain before vomiting, psoas sign (lay patient on left side and, with knee straight, extend right hip, positive if abdominal pain increases) are the best symptoms to rule in appendicitis when present. Absence of pain before vomiting is strong evidence against appendicitis.
Cholecystitis: typically patients have RUQ pain and Murphy's sign. For diagnosing choledocholithiasis, nausea and constant epigastric pain radiating to the back were described by most patients in one case series. The Tokyo guideline for acute cholecystitis of elevated CRP level (3 mg/dl or more) with ultrasonographic findings suggesting acute cholecystitis has a positive predictive value of 95% and can be used as a tool to aid diagnosis. Dissecting abdominal aortic aneurysm: patients may have sudden onset of severe sharp pain (ripping or tearing in 50%), male gender, history of hypertension, a new murmur, associated syncope (rare), pulsatile abdominal mass (rare), or asymmetric pulses (minority of patients). Racial differences in presentation were reported in one study using an international case registry. Blacks were 10 years younger at presentation and more likely to have a history of cocaine abuse, hypertension and diabetes than whites. In addition, blacks were less likely to have hypotension, shock, or tamponade and more likely to have acute kidney failure than their white counterparts but had similar in-hospital mortality (14.3% vs 19.1%, respectively). Diverticulitis: typically patients have LLQ pain and tenderness. Palpatory tenderness only in the LLQ has the highest positive likelihood ratio (LR+ 10.4). Ectopic pregnancy: typically patients are women of childbearing age with lower quadrant pain and vaginal bleeding. Likelihood of ectopic pregnancy is increased with uterine size of 8 weeks or less, history of tubal ligation, peritoneal signs, and history of infertility or intrauterine device (IUD) use. Intestinal obstruction: constipation, vomiting relieving the pain, history of abdominal surgery, abnormal bowel sounds, and abdominal distention and rigidity all moderately increase the likelihood of bowel obstruction when present. All are fairly nonsensitive, so the absence of any one does not significantly reduce the likelihood of obstruction. Mesenteric ischemia: typical patients have pain out of proportion to examination and a history of vascular disease or thrombotic disease. A small proportion may have no prior history of vascular disease and are at increased risk following cardiac surgery with extracorporeal circulation or when on vasopressors. Pancreatitis: typically patients have epigastric pain radiating to the back, vomiting, fever, and a history of alcoholism or gallbladder disease. Other less common precipitating factors include hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia and medications. Pelvic inflammatory disease: typically patients have lower quadrant pain, bilateral tenderness, vaginal discharge, cervical motion tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, no migration of pain, and no nausea or vomiting. Urinary tract infection (pyelonephritis or cystitis): typically patients report dysuria and/or hematuria, have no vaginal symptoms, and may believe they have a urinary tract infection (UTI). Urolithiasis: typically patients have flank pain and hematuria. Pain from ureterolithiasis tends to be colicky, radiating to the groin and recurs after minutes to hours. In equivocal cases, use a clinical decision rule to determine whether the patient is high risk for urolithiasis.
Pain usually of more than 48 hours duration :
Dyspepsia (ulcer- or non-ulcer-related gastritis): patients have chronic or recurrent pain or discomfort centered in the upper abdomen in relation to a meal. Symptoms that are most useful to rule in ulcer when present are food reduces pain, night waking + food relief, and episodic pain. However, no individual symptom is very helpful. GERD: patients complain of heartburn, regurgitation, often after meals, aggravated by recumbent position or bending over, and relieved by antacids. Irritable bowel syndrome: patients typically have abdominal discomfort associated with altered bowel function, a chronic course, and a normal examination. This is diagnosed accurately with Rome IV criteria. Other criteria such as the Manning criteria have fallen out of favor. Abdominal wall pain: The pain may be due to a nerve entrapment, abdominal muscle injury or from a hernia. Pain emanating from the abdomen can be distinguished from pain due to the abdominal viscera by the Carnett sign. Pain that remains unchanged or increases when the patient tenses their abdominal muscles (positive Carnett test) is likely to be an adominal wall-associated pathology (LR+ 2.9, 95% CI 2.7-3.1 and LR− 0.2, 95% CI 0.1-0.3) or abdominal wall pain (LR+ 2.6, 95% CI 2.4-2.8 and LR− 0.2, 95% CI 0.13-0.4).

Abdominal pain may also be due to extra-abdominal causes including myocardial infarction and pneumonia. A good history and physical exam will help direct the appropriate investigations in these instances.
The most reliable diagnostic tests for each of the most common causes of abdominal pain are given in and .

The American College of Radiology (ACR 2018) recommends computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis with contrast as usually appropriate for patients with acute nonlocalized abdominal pain and fever but no recent surgery. For patients without fever, either CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with contrast or without are usually appropriate.

listitem.em: Pain usually of less than 48 hours duration:

list.listitem: Appendicitis: order a CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast if the diagnosis is less than certain. Use the Alvarado scoring system to determine whether a CT would help in an equivocal case of suspected appendicitis. A score of 7 or higher makes appendicitis very likely; consult with a surgeon. Patients with scores of 4 to 6 should undergo CT scanning. Patients with a score of 3 or lower have a very low incidence (3.7%) of appendicitis, and close follow-up or imaging are good options. An elevated bilirubin (>1.0 mg/dl) can be helpful in diagnosing a ruptured appendix (LR+ 5).

Multidetector CT in an adult has a very high positive likelihood ratio (LR+ 51.3) for appendicitis. Authors of a Cochrane review found a summary sensitivity for CT of 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96), specificity of 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.95), probability of appendicitis following a positive CT of 0.92 (95% CI 0.90-0.94) and probability of having appendicitis following a negative CT result of 0.04 (95% CI 0.03-0.05) using a median prevalence of appendicitis of 0.43. In a systematic review, use of CT for cases of suspected appendicitis resulted in a negative appendectomy rate of 8.7% vs 16.7% using clinical evaluation alone (P <.001). In a study of adolescents with nontraumatic abdominal pain, contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for diagnosis of appendicitis performed similarly to CT (for both tests, sensitivity 93.6% and specificity 94.3%).

If CT is unavailable or in pregnant women, consider graded compression ultrasound (US).Authors of a meta-analysis of 17 studies with 2385 patients concluded that point-of-care US was reasonably sensitive and specific for diagnosing appendicitis with a LR+ of 9.3 (95% CI 4.8-18.4) and a LR- of 0.18 (95% CI 0.08-0.33). US performed even better among children, with a LR+ 19.4 (5-99), and LR- 0.05 (0.0-0.29).

In a prospective study of adult patients with abdominal pain and suspected appendicitis presenting to the emergency department, a normal total white blood cell count (WBC) or normal absolute neutrophil count (ANC) combined with a normal proprietary C-reactive protein (pCRP) was useful in ruling out appendicitis. In this study of 422 patients, of whom 19.1% had acute appendicitis, a normal WBC and pCRP had a sensitivity of 97.5% (95% CI 91.3-99.3%), an NPV of 98.8% (95% CI 95.9-99.7%) and a specificity of 50.0% (95% CI 44.7-55.3%) for acute appendicitis. A normal ANC and pCRP had a sensitivity of 100% (95% CI 95.4-100%), a negative predictive value of 100% (95% CI 97.5-100%) and a specificity of 44.4% (95% CI 39.2-49.7%) for acute appendicitis.

For women of childbearing age with acute lower abdominal pain, nonspecific lower abdominal pain or suspected appendicitis, authors of a Cochrane review found laparoscopy vs. open appendectomy resulted in an increased rate of specific diagnoses but no difference in adverse events.

Cholecystitis: abdominal ultrasound is the best test. Laboratory examinations are not very helpful although NICE recommends offering liver function testing along with ultrasound (US) to patients with suspected gallstone disease. In children, US appears to have lower sensitivities and positive predictive values than those reported in adults. This may be due to the higher percentage of children with chronic vs acute cholecystitis.

Cholescintigraphy using 99mTC-hepatic iminodiacetic acid (HIDA scan) is indicated if an ultrasound is not diagnostic. Technetium-labeled HIDA is injected intravenously and is then taken up selectively by hepatocytes and excreted into bile. If the cystic duct is patent, the tracer will enter the gallbladder, leading to its visualization. Nonvisualization of the gallbladder is diagnostic of acute cholecystitis. This occurs because of cystic duct obstruction, usually from edema associated with acute cholecystitis or an obstructing stone. HIDA scan has a sensitivity and specificity for acute cholecystitis of approximately 90 to 97 percent and 71 to 90 percent, respectively.

Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) can be considered if US has not detected common bile duct stones but the bile duct is dilated and/or liver function test results are abnormal. If this test is inconclusive, an endoscopic US can be considered. When complications of cholecystitis are suspected such as gangrene, gallstone ileus and perforation, CT of the abdomen is the appropriate imaging test.

Dissecting abdominal aortic aneurysm: if the diagnosis is uncertain and the patient is stable, aortic ultrasound is the best first choice. If you are fairly certain of the diagnosis and urgent surgery may be needed, order a helical CT with contrast (CTA) or MRA, as these better evaluate the full extent of the aneurysm. Unstable patients in whom the diagnosis is likely should be promptly resuscitated and go directly to the operating room.
Diverticulitis: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and IV contrast is the best test.
Ectopic pregnancy: order a urine pregnancy test. If positive, order a transvaginal US as well as a quantitative β-chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) test.

Intestinal obstruction: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast (only) is the best test, but supine and upright abdomen x-ray is a close second. In one study, there was no improvement in diagnostic accuracy when including erect radiographs with supine radiographs for adult patients with suspected bowel obstruction or paralytic ileus, although intra- and inter-rater agreement improved when using both tests. MRI and ultrasound were also found to be accurate in diagnosing small bowel obstruction. Positive likelihood ratios in this systematic review for CT, MRI and ultrasound were 3.6 (5- to 10-mm slices, 95% CI 2.3-5.4), 6.8 (95% CI 2.1-21.5), and 14.1 (95% CI 3.6-55.7), respectively.

Mesenteric ischemia: if the patient has a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT) or a known hypercoagulable state, order CTA to rule out mesenteric venous thrombosis. Multidetector CT is reasonably sensitive but not highly specific for acute mesenteric ischemia (LR+ 5.4, LR− 0.08). An elevated lactate has a high sensitivity for mesenteric ischemia (90% sensitive). However, a normal lactic acid level does not rule out mesenteric ischemia. If there is a high index of suspicion then a CT angiogram of the abdomen is indicated.

A prolonged prothombin time may help discriminate between spontaneous intramural intestinal hemorrhage and acute mesenteric ischemia, as CT may show similar findings. Intestinal fatty acid binding protein had moderate diagnostic accuracy for intestinal ischemia with an area under the curve of 0.82, 95% CI 0.79-0.86 based on a meta-analysis of 10 studies with 1265 patients; risk of selection bias was high.

Pancreatitis: order lipase and amylase tests. Elevated lipase or amylase are sensitive in diagnosis and a level >3x the upper limit of normal is required. Amylase has a short half life and the diagnosis may be missed in patients presenting after 24 hours of onset of symptoms. Lipase has a longer half life and is the preferred test. Order an ultrasound US to detect gallbladder stones on patients with acute pancreatitis. Use CT scan abdomen and pelvis with contrast or MRI without IV contrast with MRCP if the cause of abdominal pain is unclear or in patients with severe disease as determined by APACHE II or Ranson's criteria.

Pelvic inflammatory disease: no testing is required to make the diagnosis and begin treatment. Wet prep negative for WBCs makes the diagnosis of pelvic inflammatory disease unlikely. Consider cervical DNA probe for gonorrhea and chlamydia organisms to confirm the diagnosis.
UTI: symptoms alone may be more reliable than U/A. Urine culture is the gold standard.

Urolithiasis: CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast is the best test (LR+ 47, LR− 0.05).Consider US if CT is not available, in pregnant women, or as a bedside screening tool; however, a negative US does not rule out a stone. Urinalysis has a poor positive and negative predictive value (60% and 73%) and should not be used alone to exclude urolithiasis.

listitem.em: Pain usually of more than 48 hours duration:

list.listitem: Dyspepsia (ulcer- or nonulcer-related gastritis): testing is usually not necessary. If patient has "alarm features" (bleeding [melena, hematochezia, hematemesis], anemia, early satiety, unexplained weight loss >10% body weight, progressive dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, family history of GI cancer, previous esophagogastric malignancy, previous documented peptic ulcer, lymphadenopathy, or abdominal mass), order an upper endoscopy. If H. pylori prevalence is 10% or more in your community, consider testing for H. pylori with stool antigen test (LR+ 9.3, LR− 0.05). Leave a 2-week washout period after proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use before testing for H. pylori.

GERD: testing is usually not necessary. A trial of high-dose proton pump inhibitor is 75% sensitive for GERD and 55% specific. If there are "alarm features" (dysphagia, odynophagia, bleeding, weight loss, anemia, symptoms lasting >5 years), order an upper endoscopy. Barium upper GI testing and Helicobacter (H.) pylori testing are not helpful.

Irritable bowel syndrome: Testing is usually not necessary. If "alarm features" (hematochezia, weight loss >10 lb, family history of colon cancer, recurring fever, anemia, chronic severe diarrhea) are present, arrange lower endoscopy. If diarrhea is predominant, consider testing for celiac disease, as its prevalence is 5% in patients with IBS compared with less than 1% in healthy controls.
Pancreatic cancer: of the imaging tests available, consider endosonographic fine needle aspiration biopsy (LR+ 14.3, LR− 0.15) or FDG-PET/CT imaging (LR+ 14.2, LR− 0.16).
A clinical rule was developed and validated to predict the likelihood of a significant cause of abdominal pain in adult men.
The Bali, Imrie, and Ranson scores help to predict the prognosis in patients with acute pancreatitis.

The Alvarado score can risk-stratify patients with suspected appendicitis and help to identify those requiring immediate surgical consultation vs those who should have imaging or close clinical follow-up.
Assess stability; arrange urgent transport of unstable patients to the hospital for resuscitation while workup continues.

Determine the duration of pain: if pain is of less than 48 hours duration, rule out an "acute abdomen" (more likely with pain followed by vomiting, age 65 years or older, history of abdominal surgery, abdominal guarding, and rebound tenderness). If you suspect an acute abdomen, consider a surgical consult.
Use of opioid analgesics for patients with acute abdominal pain makes them more comfortable and is unlikely to interfere with diagnosis.

Use historical and physical examination clues to direct you toward a presumptive diagnosis (see and ). When pain is localized to the right upper or lower quadrants, ultrasound is the preferred initial diagnostic test.

If the etiology is still unclear, but immediately dangerous diagnoses are unlikely, consider reassuring the patient and arranging close follow-up. A clinical decision rule can help determine the likelihood that serious disease is present.

algorithm.title: Abdominal Pain of Less than 48 Hours Duration: Diagnosis.

cell.label: Presume ectopic pregnancy TV US + quantitative β-HCG.
Presume diverticulitis: CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV/oral contrast.
Presume urolithiasis: CT of abdomen and pelvis without contrast.
Presume appendicitis: If equivocal, CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.
Presume intestinal obstruction: CT of abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast.
Presume AAA: imaging if diagnosis in question or preop if patient stable, OR if unstable.
Pain out of proportion to examination?
Presume mesenteric ischemia: CT angiogram, lactic acid level, or abdominal angiogram (see Diagnostic Tests table).
Presume pancreatitis: obtain lipase and amylase levels If positive, then US of abdomen.
